newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Optus Vision CEO steps down, says battles won.
newsitem.headline: Optus Vision CEO steps down, says battles won.

text.p: Cable TV network Optus Vision had successfully challenged Rupert Murdoch's dominance of Australian pay television, said its chief executive on Thursday before announcing he would shortly step down.
Geoffrey Cousins said he would relinquish his position as chief executive and take up the chairmanship of the company within the next few months.
"As far as the major strategic battles are concerned they're over and as a pay television operator Optus Vision is absolutely in the winning position," Cousins told a news conference.
Cousins, speaking one year after the launch of Optus Vision's service, also announced better-than-expected subscriber figures of more than 100,000.

While this is still just below the 115,000 claimed by the Murdoch-backed Foxtel pay TV service, Optus has a higher subscriber pickup rate from its cabling, which is potentially available to more than a million homes, mainly on the east coast of the country.

Foxtel's other partner is Australian government-owned telecommunications group Telstra Corp, which foots the bill for the A$4.00 billion (US$3.16 billion) cable rollout that carries Foxtel programmes and Telstra's telephony service.
Cousins, a former advertising executive, joined Optus Vision early last year to oversee its A$3.5 billion fibre-optic cable rollout and launch of the TV and telephone businesses.
During his stay, he has engaged in several battles with Murdoch and Foxtel over sports and movie programming.
The most notable clash was over the coverage of Rugby League, one of Australia's most popular sports.

Optus Vision, aligned with media tycoon Kerry Packer and the ruling body of the sport, the Australian Rugby League (ARL), won the contest after Murdoch's planned breakaway competition known as 'SuperLeague' was banned by the courts until 2000.

"All of those things have been head-on fights," Cousins told reporters. "They have been the big fights in this business and I would like to put it to you that we have not lost any of those fights and I think that is important.

"When we formed this business, a lot of people said 'you just can't beat Rupert Murdoch, you just can't beat News (Corp) and you just can't beat Telstra' -- and they are not unreasonable statements," Cousins said.
"But I think the jury is now in after those big strategic issues. They are resolved and they are not resolved in favour of our competitors."
But the fight is not over.

Foxtel is due to appeal the 'SuperLeague' decision at the end of the month and around the same time Optus Vision plans to challenge News Corp's rights to the broadcast of Australian rugby union games.
The struggle to win Australian pay TV viewers has been costly, with the three market operators making total losses of about A$575 million in the year to June 30.
The biggest loss was recorded by satellite TV operator Australis Media Ltd, which posted a loss of A$251.7 million.
Cousins' career switch took the market by surprise.
"It is an odd announcement, maybe he has just decided to take it easy for a while and play a bit more golf," one Sydney-based telecommunications analyst said.
Optus Vision is 46.5 percent owned by both Australian telecommunications carrier Optus Communications and Continental CableVision Inc, which has merged with U.S. West.
The balance is owned by Seven Network Ltd and Kerry Packer's Publishing and Broadcasting Ltd.
